Senses.Explanation: The line belongs to Dongshan’s water-reflection verse: ‘Everywhere I meet him; he is now exactly me; I am now not him.’ Later records keep the pair in play rather than flattening it into identity. An unnamed monk asks Yingning what the first half means and is warned not to taste water in a land of poison; another monk offers the pair as a comment and Sanyi asks where its fault lies; Tianran names the verse as the source from which the Five Ranks issue while rejecting fixed theoretical elaboration. The entry therefore preserves the pronouns and the paired asymmetry instead of resolving them into a doctrine.

Senses.Note: Dongshan's verse on seeing his reflection says that the other is precisely himself, then refuses the reverse identification. Wuyi explains the pair through the five positions, and Yingning rejects the reading that turns the image into a permanent inner self. Shiyu explicitly names Dongshan after the pair and critiques his formulation. Other masters answer with verses or use the pair in direct instruction about seeing, seeking, and meeting. The two clauses must be held together: the first permits recognition, while the second prevents the reflected figure from becoming a fixed self.

Wuyi's address quotes Dongshan's complete verse, beginning with the warning against seeking from another and ending with accord with suchness. He then repeats these two lines as a stringent test: what is the 'he' that is precisely me, what is the 'I' that is not him, and are they one or two? He says the responses of all five houses must pass through this test, before turning to three kinds of leakage. Dongshan is the quoted verse voice; Wuyi owns the ensuing questions and instruction. The repeated lines within this large window therefore include Wuyi's active examination of the quotation, not a second historical speech by Dongshan.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J26/J26nB188.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Rujiu Ruibai. In his reply from Longhua to the literary man Xing Jixian, Ruibai welcomes the correspondent's apparent entry but asks whether his confidence is complete. If it is, he should recognize these two lines and accord with suchness. Ruibai immediately prevents that recognition from becoming a resting place: making a livelihood within suchness would still be confinement in a brocade prison, with another fetter attached. He asks how one would get free and points to further opening. Here the inherited verse is Ruibai's present test of a correspondent, rather than a fresh narrative of Dongshan's reflection.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB190.xml). Dharma Platform of Chan Master Shiyu. Shiyu's address concerns a lineage grandson who enters the mountain to thank his teacher after completing mourning. Images of spring weather, spiritual kinship, and meeting 'him' lead into the two quoted lines. Shiyu then names old Dongshan and criticizes the two sides with the images of adding a head upon a head and cutting off a head to seek life. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB300.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chaozong. Chaozong raises the story of the woman born at the same time as the Buddha who refuses to see him, yet sees him in every direction and even between her fingers when covering her face. He asks the intent of not wanting to see the Buddha and answers with these two lines. For the unavoidable seeing, he supplies another line from Dongshan's verse, going alone and meeting him everywhere. He then contrasts her unsuccessful avoidance with the assembly's unsuccessful search and asks where the fault lies, ending after a pause with contrasting images of brilliant light and overwhelming waves. The headword is Chaozong's present application, not the woman's speech.

Wuyi's address quotes Dongshan's complete verse, beginning with the warning against seeking from another and ending with accord with suchness. He then repeats these two lines as a stringent test: what is the 'he' that is precisely me, what is the 'I' that is not him, and are they one or two? He says the responses of all five houses must pass through this test, before turning to three kinds of leakage. Dongshan is the quoted verse voice; Wuyi owns the ensuing questions and instruction. The repeated lines within this large window therefore include Wuyi's active examination of the quotation, not a second historical speech by Dongshan.

Shiyu's address concerns a lineage grandson who enters the mountain to thank his teacher after completing mourning. Images of spring weather, spiritual kinship, and meeting 'him' lead into the two quoted lines. ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB300.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Chaozong. Chaozong raises the story of the woman born at the same time as the Buddha who refuses to see him, yet sees him in every direction and even between her fingers when covering her face. He asks the intent of not wanting to see the Buddha and answers with these two lines. For the unavoidable seeing, he supplies another line from Dongshan's verse, going alone and meeting him everywhere. He then contrasts her unsuccessful avoidance with the assembly's unsuccessful search and asks where the fault lies, ending after a pause with contrasting images of brilliant light and overwhelming waves. The headword is Chaozong's present application, not the woman's speech.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 正於夷俟時訶責之。幼而不孫弟，禮不為我輩設也；長而無述，為谿為谷也；老而不死，出死入生也。三者乃原壤生平大得意處，此不過自了漢，故呼之為賊。狄梁公事女主，日夜苦心，指天誓日，只有廬陵一案，若貌似蓮花之六郎，一切穢濁不堪直視之狗彘，此大聖大賢事主處友之機權。故曰：君子見其遠者大者，小人見其小者近者。即衲子輩事師交友，亦須別具一隻參學眼。潘達曰：「亦有小處近處極關係者。」仰之彌高章仰之彌高章高堅前後認為歎道者固錯，謂歎自家工夫無捉摸者亦錯。顏子初時不知道之在我，只將我去求道，又認作聖人可以一蹴而至，嘗自云：「夫子步亦步，趨亦趨，夫子絕塵而奔，回且瞠乎其後。」只遮瞠乎其後處，正是出身活路，不知卻坐在此處，反以為不及，此是學道通病。待得夫子拽轉他鼻頭來，始覺開眼也是，合眼也是，方悟夫子循循善誘，博我者還是我自家的文，約我者還是我自家的禮，到遮裏不能親自見我，便罷手不得，直是聰明才智一毫用不著。斯時於山窮水盡處瞥地開眼，原來只在遮裏，所謂渠今正是我，我今不是渠，如有所立卓爾，雖欲從而末由，正是放身命處，不復如從前向外馳求，乃知為人由己而由人乎底意方透，可謂極善形容。自述悟由始終得力行狀，特地與夫子拈此一瓣香，以酬直指我心一點法乳之恩耳。使非萬分勇猛於反己，何能至是哉？是以顏氏子歿，夫子不勝歎息曰：「惜乎！吾見其進，未見其止。」使顏子不死，而遇人逢時，又不知作何大事業。以德報怨章以德報怨章以德報怨，此大聖人事，亦老氏之言也。彼見當時瞋毒熾盛，睚眥殺人，思以救之。譬如人患熱病，將冷水當頭一潑，暫時得蘇，熱終內伏。不若夫子先與提清脈絡，曰：「何以報德？」又向德中揭出直，直中揭出德，又玅於怨中揭出直來。不揭出直來，則天下盡陷於不仁不義，無一人能存性生之直也。夫子嘗云：「詩可以怨。」怨者，天地之義氣。立己處人，有一毫不合於德義，則自怨自艾，自不容己。艾，藥也。人無恥而不自怨，則是大聖拱手，不可救藥之人也。不知怨，則不知興，并不知德矣。立個方便，曰：以直報怨，以德報德。蓋犯而無校，橫逆必反，此克己強恕事，不可以恩怨一概溷濫。記曰：君父之仇，不共戴天；兄弟之仇，不反兵而鬥；朋友之仇，主人能則執兵隨其後，是之為直。直是吾心之天理生性，不可滅也。人無此，則彼此倫常絕矣。賴天有怨報之直，故天下多不敢

In the ancestral unit headed for Dongshan Liangjie, the record moves from his exchange with Yunyan about insentient preaching to his later awakening on seeing his reflection while crossing water. Dongshan's complete verse includes these two lines and the final instruction to accord with suchness. Baiyu's own following poem begins by complicating the image: seeing the reflection and meeting 'him' is not simply 'him'; once home, why need a message carried by a goose? It continues with dawn, plum blossom, and moonlit imagery. The quoted headword and Baiyu's response must remain separate voices; the next ancestral unit is Yunju's.
ClaimAnchors.ClaimText: 渠今正是我，我今不是渠

Senses.Explanation: Dongshan's verse says, 'He now is precisely me; I now am not him.' Its two clauses deliberately resist a simple equation: recognition does not make the two pronouns interchangeable. In the crossing-water narratives the words follow his seeing his reflection, but the retained later uses do more than describe a reflected image. Wuyi asks what each pronoun means and whether they are one or two; Ruibai uses the lines to test a correspondent's confidence and then warns against settling even in suchness. Chaozong applies them to the woman who refuses to see the Buddha, while Juelang brings them into an account of learning from Confucius. Yingning explicitly attacks an interpretation that turns the pronouns into a fixed division between an original person and an everyday person. His polemic is evidence of a contested reading, not an explanation the entry adopts. The occurrence notes distinguish Dongshan's quoted verse from each later master's question, criticism, poem, or application.

Senses.PreferredTarget: He likes being laughed at; you fear being laughed at
AlternateTargets: He welcomes another's laugh, while you are afraid of it
SearchAliases: Yangqi likes laughter you fear laughter
he loves being laughed at you fear it
Senses.Note: Baiyun Shouduan is unsettled by Yangqi's response to his earlier verse. Yangqi answers that the other person likes being laughed at whereas Shouduan fears it, and Shouduan awakens in the transmitted encounter. Yinyuan, Jizong, Foyuan, and Yanju add independent comments or verses on the force of the laugh. The exact paired rebuke is Yangqi's, not those later writers'.

Senses.Explanation: He and I is the compact pronoun pair used in Dongshan's river verse and the Precious Mirror Composure to articulate the relation 'he is not I; I precisely am he.' Caodong writers say the two graphs organize upright and biased, light and dark, ruler and minister, and cite Dongshan's crossing-water awakening. Juelang Daosheng calls their interpenetration the basis from which the Five Ranks were established. Oxherding verses also say the feelings of he and I are forgotten. That remains the same relational pronoun pair, though deployed outside the Dongshan technical analysis.

Senses.PreferredTarget: He has no land of his own; where could you meet him?
AlternateTargets: If he has no realm, where is there a place to encounter him?
SearchAliases: he has no land where to meet him

Senses.Note: A monk asks Shishuang how to see Buddha after brushing away dust. Shishuang replies that the one sought has no land, then asks where he could be met. Later masters compare this with Jiashan on the same question or use the pair to answer a present seeker. The first clause removes a fixed realm; the second turns the search itself into a question. It is not a claim that a person must travel elsewhere to find him. The final retained headword is Songxu's question, answered by Yuanjie; other repeated Shishuang case witnesses remain quoted old turns within later masters' commentary.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J34/J34nB298.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shenfeng Xian. Shenfeng Xian asks what remains when the names Buddha and ancestor are removed. He lists Yunmen's dried shit-stick, Dongshan's three pounds of flax, Zhaozhou's cypress, and Linji's no-rank true person, then rejects the whole list. Waving the whisk, he allows that the figure in Zhaozhou's hall is somewhat different: praise, slander, offerings and abuse are all possible. The inherited line belongs to Shishuang Qingzhu's transmission, while Shenfeng is the present commentator applying it. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J27/J27nB189.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Sanyi Yu. Sanyi Mingyu speaks of the five positions and the relation of ruler and minister, then insists that what is used must be one's own: a household treasure is not acquired outside. He evokes jewel trees, golden stairs, jade halls and towers, then abruptly asks with the headword where one could meet him if he has no country. Calling to the assembly, Sanyi names four disciples of Confucius and shouts. Sanyi owns this present use of the inherited pair. Yezhu Fuhui retells the monk asking Jiashan and Shishuang about brushing away dust to see Buddha. Jiashan prescribes wielding a sword; Shishuang gives the headword. When the monk reports back, Jiashan weighs the two responses in terms of teaching arrangements and deep discussion of principle. Yezhu then says that if someone put the same question to him today, he would strike across the spine immediately. He asks whether that would be an arrangement of the teaching courtyard or deep discussion of principle, and demands a quick answer. The headword remains Shishuang's quoted reply; Yezhu owns the proposed blow and the demand that follows. His present challenge prevents the two inherited descriptions from becoming a finished classification.

He lists Yunmen's dried shit-stick, Dongshan's three pounds of flax, Zhaozhou's cypress, and Linji's no-rank true person, then rejects the whole list. Waving the whisk, he allows that the figure in Zhaozhou's hall is somewhat different: praise, slander, offerings and abuse are all possible. He asks why and cites the old line, 'He has no land of his own; where could you meet him?' The inherited line belongs to Shishuang Qingzhu's transmission, while Shenfeng is the present commentator applying it. Here it closes the question of locating someone through names or appraisals; Shenfeng does not identify a new geographical country to replace the rejected names.

Sanyi Mingyu speaks of the five positions and the relation of ruler and minister, then insists that what is used must be one's own: a household treasure is not acquired outside. He evokes jewel trees, golden stairs, jade halls and towers, then abruptly asks with the headword where one could meet him if he has no country. Calling to the assembly, Sanyi names four disciples of Confucius and shouts. Sanyi owns this present use of the inherited pair. It interrupts the sumptuous landscape he has just evoked, so that those images cannot by themselves supply the residence being sought. The record does not assign a concealed meaning to each jewel or named disciple.

He then gives his own alternative, using the Buddha's curled hair, hand markings and lotus-supported feet, and asks whether it is the same as or different from the elders. Shishuang owns the quoted headword, not Wuyi. Wuyi's application asks his assembly to account for the difference between replies instead of treating the no-country answer as the only permissible wording.

Wu cites the Surangama scripture: when one person returns to the source, the worlds in the ten directions disappear. He asks where one could stand then. Yingning first answers with a strange lock image, a lock without whiskers shaking at both ends. Wu says that his doubt has increased, and Yingning replies with the headword. Wu bows gladly and leaves. The pair answers Wu's demand for a location after the disappearance described in his quotation. The text records his pleased departure without separately declaring him awakened or explaining the earlier lock image.

Senses.Explanation: The second line of a four-line verse attributed to Shiqi Buddha, in which harmful karma too is called illusion. The original verse is preserved in Zutang Ji. Yushan, Chuiwan, Zhean, and Shengren each apply or interpret this line in their own discourse. Chuiwan challenges action after quoting the Shiqi verse; Zhean applies the illusion claim to a current memorial sermon; Shengren presses the distinction between real and illusory in another current memorial sermon.
